papers.title: Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?
papers.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. However, most of them adopt a step-by-step interaction paradigm where the current visual observation is sent to the agent before each action. In practical deployment, this paradigm introduces two fundamental limitations: the game loop must wait for model inference, making real-time interaction impractical, and repeated VLM calls incur substantial cost. Therefore, we propose PlayScriptBench, a script-based game benchmark that evaluates whether VLMs can synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states. This setting jointly evaluates visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategic reasoning, and executable program synthesis, providing a more comprehensive assessment of game-playing agents. To support more tractable evaluation for current general-purpose VLMs, we further introduce a four-stage pipeline --- Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition --- that decomposes controller synthesis into game exploration, state perception, interface construction, and strategic control, enabling agents to progressively construct an executable program. Experiments on 16 games spanning 4 genres show that even strong VLMs struggle on our benchmark, revealing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop game control. These results establish script-based controller synthesis as a complementary direction for benchmarking VLM-based game-playing agents.

authors.name: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Dingyu Zhang, Jianqiang Huang

papers.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
papers.summary: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across closed and open-source models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

authors.name: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang

papers.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

authors.name: Huanran Li, Nhat X. T. Le, Kevin De Angeli, Yao Xuan, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic

papers.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
papers.summary: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B-14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs), and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.

authors.name: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma, Xuanning Cao

papers.title: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models
papers.summary: In text to image AI models, fixing the prompt and the random seed is widely assumed to fix the image. We show that it does not on GPUs. We evaluate six text-to-image models (diffusion and autoregressive) under four numerical precisions and quantizations on three GPU types (RTX A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, and H100 NVL), across up to 100 prompts per set for all six models. For each configuration we compare, with the prompt and seed fixed, the image generated alone with the image generated inside a batch, and we also compare across GPUs. Every replay control reported here is bit-exact, so the variation is not random noise: the execution setting, mainly the batch composition and the GPU, decides the output. The effect is large and model dependent. Structural similarity between the single-image and the batched output falls to 0.580 for an autoregressive model in bf16 and to 0.551 with int8. For a second autoregressive model in bf16 it falls to 0.261 with sampled decoding and to 0.229 with greedy decoding, and for an fp8 diffusion model to 0.68. A diffusion model in bf16 stays close to the batch-1 output (0.96-0.98) but changes every image. In most cases the batched image is a different but equally valid image; in some, such as prompts with digits and counters, it is visibly worse. Cross-GPU differences are of the same order as the batch effect: for one autoregressive model in bf16 compared across two GPU architectures (RTX 6000 Ada versus RTX A6000), no image is bit-identical and the cross-GPU LPIPS (0.355 to 0.383) matches the batch effect within one GPU (0.347 to 0.381). The consequences are direct: seeds do not make results reproducible, benchmarks and image-quality comparisons that mix batch sizes or hardware can be biased, and safety audits and A/B tests on generated images need the serving setup reported.

authors.name: Javier Conde, Xiuyuan Qi, Shanshan Liu, Pedro Reviriego

papers.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
papers.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

authors.name: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume

papers.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
papers.summary: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

authors.name: Qian Chen, Kun Zhu, Zhongyi Wang, Ling Chen

papers.title: EffectWAM: Learning Action-Grounded Effects for Robot Manipulation
papers.summary: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.

authors.name: Yuan Zhang, Hao Cui, Jingfei Ni, Meiyi Wang, Xin Nie, Chi Liu, Wenjie Xu, Lin Gao, Hao Li, Xianhe Zhang, Jiajia Wu, Diyuan Liu, Jia Pan, Chao Ji

papers.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
papers.summary: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

authors.name: Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh, Byung-Jun Lee

papers.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
papers.summary: A generative verifier can flag an unsupported claim before it finishes describing the error. For applications that only screen an assistant's report, the remaining generation may be unnecessary. We examine this possibility in a frozen 2B span verifier whose output chooses between an empty error list and its first object before producing any locations. Native8 stops at that choice. Prefill1 supplies the seven fixed syntax tokens that precede it and generates just the unrestricted branch token, keeping the native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 uses 84.84% less eager resident service than full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It also saves 31.98% over Native8 despite identical logical token totals. This additional saving remains 6.74-26.73% under default compiled execution on the complete workload, with small changes in decisions. Evidence interventions test whether the alarm responds to the supplied facts; first-location decoding measures the additional work and localization losses when a caller also needs an error pointer.

authors.name: Yanbin Gong, Lei Chen

papers.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
papers.summary: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.

authors.name: Justin Dumouchelle, Esther Julien, Jannis Kurtz, Elias B. Khalil

papers.title: Polyrating: A Cost-Effective and Bias-Aware Rating System for LLM Evaluation
papers.summary: Rating-based human evaluation has become an essential tool to accurately evaluate the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs). However, current rating systems suffer from several important limitations: first, they fail to account for biases that significantly influence evaluation results, second, they require large and expensive preference datasets to obtain accurate ratings, and third, they do not facilitate meaningful comparisons of model ratings across different tasks. To address these issues, we introduce Polyrating, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs. Polyrating can detect and quantify biases affecting human preferences, ensuring fairer model comparisons. Further, Polyrating can reduce the cost of human evaluations by up to $59\%$ for new models and up to $77\%$ for new tasks by leveraging existing benchmark scores. Lastly, Polyrating enables direct comparisons of ratings across different tasks, providing a comprehensive understanding of an LLMs' strengths, weaknesses, and relative performance across different applications.

authors.name: Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev

papers.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
papers.summary: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

authors.name: Leah von der Heyde, Anna-Carolina Haensch, Alexander Wenz, Bolei Ma

papers.title: Fine-Grained Instruction-Guided Graph Reasoning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.summary: Vision and Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to traverse complex environments by following natural language instructions, demanding accurate alignment between visual observations and linguistic guidance. To address these challenges, we propose a fine grained instruction guided graph reasoning framework (FIGR) that enhances both spatial representation and instruction understanding during navigation. Specifically, an observation graph interaction mechanism is introduced to disentangle angular and visual cues while strengthening directed edge representations through geometric embedding, enabling more reliable spatial reasoning within the navigation graph. The key detail guidance module is implemented as Adaptive Open Vocabulary Guidance (AOVG), where a contextual role parser dynamically identifies location, object, spatial relation, and other contextual cues. This design avoids exact string matching and supports previously unseen entities and compositional expressions. For multilingual instructions, a Multilingual Semantic Adapter (MSA) maps language-specific representations into a shared navigation-semantic space. By jointly integrating structured graph reasoning with instruction critical semantic cues, the proposed approach significantly improves the agent ability to follow complex navigation instructions. On the validation-unseen splits, FIGR achieves 67 SPL on R2R and 64.8 sDTW on RxR, exceeding SPENav by 1 percentage point in SPL and PRET by 2.4 points in sDTW, respectively.

authors.name: Yaohua Liu, Binkai Ou, Xinyuan Song, Rong Fu, Amir H. Gandomi, Simon Fong

papers.title: DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs
papers.summary: Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM) is crucial for software development and Architectural Decision Records (ADR), an important artifact of AKM, provide a structured approach to capture Architectural Design Decisions (ADD). However, their adoption is limited due to the manual effort involved and insufficient tool support. Prior work shows that LLMs can support ADD generation, though basic prompting yields suboptimal results. This paper explores how LLMs can support architects in two complementary tasks: generating ADDs from Decision Contexts, and generating complete ADRs from titles. We propose Domain-specific Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Tuning (DRAFT), a novel approach that integrates Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Generation with Fine-tuning to generate. DRAFT operates in two phases: an offline phase that fine-tunes a model using retrieval-augmented prompts derived from historical ADRs, and an online phase that generates decisions or complete ADRs by combining retrieved examples with the fine-tuned model. Evaluated on 4344 ADRs across multiple LLMs using standard NLP metrics, DRAFT consistently produces outputs better aligned with real-world ADRs. A human evaluation with the authors and external architects, however, shows no uniformly preferred approach. DRAFT also maintains practical efficiency, reduces dependence- dence on proprietary models, and addresses organizational concerns around privacy, resource constraints, and inference costs.

authors.name: Rudra Dhar, Adyansh Kakran, Amey Karan, Vasudeva Varma, Karthik Vaidhyanathan

papers.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
papers.summary: Deep reinforcement learning can seamlessly transfer agile locomotion and navigation skills from the simulator to real world. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization or adversarial methods often demands expert physics knowledge to ensure policy robustness. Even so, cutting-edge simulators may fall short of capturing every real-world detail, and the reconstructed environment may introduce errors due to various perception uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a novel framework that employs conditional score-based diffusion models to calibrate simulator physical coefficients and residual fidelity domains online during robot execution. Specifically, the residual fidelity reflects the simulation model shift relative to the real-world dynamics and captures the uncertainty of the perceived environment, enabling us to sample realistic environments under the inferred distribution for policy fine-tuning. Our framework is informative and adaptive in three key ways: (a) we fine-tune the pretrained policy only under anomalous scenarios, (b) we build sequential NFC online with the pretrained NFC's proposal prior, reducing the diffusion model's training burden, and (c) when NFC uncertainty is high and may degrade policy improvement, we leverage optimistic exploration to enable hallucinated policy optimization. Our framework achieves superior simulator calibration precision compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse robots with high-dimensional parametric spaces. We study the critical contribution of residual fidelity to policy improvement in simulation and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust robot navigation under challenging real-world conditions, such as a broken wheel axle on snowy surfaces.

authors.name: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu

papers.title: PLAICraft: Large-Scale Time-Aligned Vision-Speech-Action Dataset for Embodied AI
papers.summary: Advances in deep generative modeling have made it increasingly plausible to train human-level embodied agents. Yet progress has been limited by the absence of large-scale, real-time, multi-modal, and socially interactive datasets that reflect the sensory-motor complexity of natural environments. To address this, we present PLAICraft, a novel data collection platform and dataset capturing multiplayer Minecraft interactions across five time-aligned modalities: video, game output audio, microphone input audio, mouse, and keyboard actions. Each modality is logged with millisecond time precision, enabling the study of synchronous, embodied behaviour in a rich, open-ended world. The dataset comprises 5525 hours of interactive gameplay from more than 232 participants. Alongside the dataset, we provide an evaluation suite for benchmarking model capabilities in object recognition, spatial awareness, language grounding, and long-term memory. PLAICraft opens a path toward training and evaluating agents that act fluently and purposefully in real time, paving the way for truly embodied artificial intelligence.

authors.name: Yingchen He, Christian D. Weilbach, Martyna E. Wojciechowska, Yiyuan Sun, Jason Yoo, Yuxuan Zhang, Oluwanifemi A. Adekanye, Chia-Hong Hsu, Vasileios Lioutas, Frank Wood

papers.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
papers.summary: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

authors.name: An Vu, Jonas Oppenlaender

papers.title: The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs
papers.summary: In recent months, large language models (LLMs) have made significant progress in mathematical proof generation, but further advancement is hindered by the lack of a large-scale, high-quality dataset of human-evaluated proofs. While expensive to create, such a dataset is essential for driving improvements in training and enabling a rigorous analysis of proof generation capabilities. In this work, we present the Open Proof Corpus (OPC), a dataset comprising over 5,000 human-evaluated proofs produced by state-of-the-art LLMs. The OPC was specifically designed for broad applicability and downstream usage in proof generation research and is the first to include a substantial number of correct, LLM-generated solutions to problems from prestigious mathematics competitions such as the USAMO and IMO. Using the OPC, we explore critical questions in automated proof generation: (1) the performance gap between natural language and formal proof generation, (2) the discrepancy between final-answer accuracy and full-proof validity, and (3) the impact of best-of-n selection on proof quality. Finally, to showcase the utility of the OPC, we finetune an 8B-parameter model on the dataset, obtaining a model that performs on par with the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, on the task of evaluating proof correctness.

authors.name: Jasper Dekoninck, Ivo Petrov, Kristian Minchev, Mislav Balunovic, Martin Vechev, Miroslav Marinov, Maria Drencheva, Lyuba Konova, Milen Shumanov, Kaloyan Tsvetkov, Nikolay Drenchev, Lazar Todorov, Kalina Nikolova, Nikolay Georgiev, Vanesa Kalinkova, Margulan Ismoldayev

papers.title: VITA: Vision-to-Action Flow Matching Policy
papers.summary: Conventional flow matching and diffusion-based policies sample via iterative denoising from standard noise distributions (e.g., Gaussian), and require conditioning modules to repeatedly incorporate visual information during the generative process, incurring substantial time and memory overhead. To reduce the complexity, we develop VITA (Vision-To-Action flow matching policy), a noise-free and conditioning-free flow matching policy learning framework that directly flows from visual representations to latent actions. Since the source of the flow is visually grounded, VITA eliminates the need for visual conditioning during generation. As expected, bridging vision and action is challenging, because actions are lower-dimensional, less structured, and sparser than visual representations; moreover, flow matching requires the source and target to have the same dimensionality. To overcome this, we introduce an action autoencoder that maps raw actions into a structured latent space aligned with visual latents, trained jointly with flow matching. To further prevent latent action space collapse during end-to-end training, we propose flow latent decoding, which anchors the latent generation process by backpropagating the action reconstruction loss through the flow matching ODE (ordinary differential equation) solving steps. We evaluate VITA on 9 simulation and 5 real-world tasks from ALOHA and Robomimic. VITA achieves 1.9x faster inference compared to conventional flow matching with conditioning modules, while outperforming or matching state-of-the-art policies. Project page: https://ucd-dare.github.io/VITA/.

authors.name: Dechen Gao, Boqi Zhao, Andrew Lee, Ian Chuang, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Zhe Zhao, Junshan Zhang, Iman Soltani

papers.title: SACA: Selective Attention-Based Clustering Algorithm
papers.summary: Clustering algorithms are fundamental tools across many fields, with density-based methods offering particular advantages in identifying arbitrarily shaped clusters and handling noise. However, their effectiveness is often limited by the requirement of critical parameter tuning by users, which typically requires significant domain expertise. This paper introduces a novel density-based clustering algorithm loosely inspired by the concept of selective attention, designed to minimize reliance on parameter tuning for most applications. The proposed method computes an adaptive threshold to exclude sparsely distributed points and outliers, constructs an initial cluster framework, and subsequently reintegrates the filtered points to refine the final results. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness, accuracy, and ease of use of the proposed approach, establishing it as a powerful alternative to conventional density-based clustering techniques.

authors.name: Meysam Shirdel Bilehsavar, Razieh Ghaedi, Christian O'Reilly

papers.title: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability. When equipped with tools through function calling and enhanced with retrieval-augmented techniques, compound LLM-based systems can access closed data sources and answer questions about them. However, they still struggle to process and reason over large-scale graph-structure data. In this technical report we introduce the GDS (Graph Data Science) agent. The GDS agent introduces a comprehensive set of graph algorithms as tools, together with preprocessing (retrieval) and postprocessing of algorithm results, in a model context protocol (MCP) server. It is accompanied by a skill that guides the LLM through graph analysis. The agent can be used with any modern LLM out-of-the-box. GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.

authors.name: Borun Shi, Lusine Adunts, Ioannis Panagiotas

papers.title: Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
papers.summary: Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.

authors.name: Michele Caprio, Mengqi Chen, Siu Lun Chau, Krikamol Muandet

papers.title: Rational Adversaries and the Maintenance of Fragility: A Game-Theoretic Theory of Rational Stagnation
papers.summary: Cooperative systems often remain in persistently suboptimal yet stable states. This paper explains such "rational stagnation" as an equilibrium sustained by a rational adversary whose utility follows the principle of potential loss, $u_{D} = U_{ideal} - U_{actual}$. Starting from the Prisoner's Dilemma, we show that the transformation $u_{i}' = a\,u_{i} + b\,u_{j}$ and the ratio of mutual recognition $w = b/a$ generate a fragile cooperation band $[w_{\min},\,w_{\max}]$ where both (C,C) and (D,D) are equilibria. Extending to a dynamic model with stochastic cooperative payoffs $R_{t}$ and intervention costs $(C_{c},\,C_{m})$, a Bellman-style analysis yields three strategic regimes: immediate destruction, rational stagnation, and intervention abandonment. The appendix further generalizes the utility to a reference-dependent nonlinear form and proves its stability under reference shifts, ensuring robustness of the framework. Applications to social-media algorithms and political trust illustrate how adversarial rationality can deliberately preserve fragility.

authors.name: Daisuke Hirota

papers.title: Shadows in the Code: Exploring the Risks and Defenses of LLM-based Multi-Agent Software Development Systems
papers.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems has significantly streamlined software developing tasks, enabling users with little technical expertise to develop executable applications. While these systems democratize software creation through natural language requirements, they introduce significant security risks that remain largely unexplored. We identify two risky scenarios: Malicious User with Benign Agents (MU-BA) and Benign User with Malicious Agents (BU-MA). We introduce the Implicit Malicious Behavior Injection Attack (IMBIA), demonstrating how multi-agent systems can be manipulated to generate software with concealed malicious capabilities beneath seemingly benign applications, and propose Adv-IMBIA as a defense mechanism. Evaluations across ChatDev, MetaGPT, and AgentVerse frameworks reveal varying vulnerability patterns, with IMBIA achieving attack success rates of 93%, 45%, and 71% in MU-BA scenarios, and 71%, 84%, and 45% in BU-MA scenarios. Our defense mechanism reduced attack success rates significantly, particularly in the MU-BA scenario. Further analysis reveals that compromised agents in the coding and testing phases pose significantly greater security risks, while also identifying critical agents that require protection against malicious user exploitation. Our findings highlight the urgent need for robust security measures in multi-agent software development systems and provide practical guidelines for implementing targeted, resource-efficient defensive strategies.

authors.name: Xiaoqing Wang, Keman Huang, Bin Liang, Hongyu Li, Xiaoyong Du

papers.title: ML-Tool-Bench: Tool-Augmented Planning for ML Tasks
papers.summary: The development of autonomous machine learning (ML) agents capable of end-to-end data science workflows represents a significant frontier in artificial intelligence. These agents must orchestrate complex sequences of data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization, tasks that require sophisticated planning and iteration. While recent work on building ML agents has explored using large language models (LLMs) for direct code generation, tool-augmented approaches offer greater modularity and reliability. However, existing tool-use benchmarks focus primarily on task-specific tool selection or argument extraction for tool invocation, failing to evaluate the sophisticated planning capabilities required for ML Agents. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented ML agents using a curated set of 61 specialized tools and 15 tabular ML challenges from Kaggle. Our benchmark goes beyond traditional tool-use evaluation by incorporating an in-memory named object management, allowing agents to flexibly name, save, and retrieve intermediate results throughout the workflows. We demonstrate that standard ReAct-style approaches struggle to generate valid tool sequences for complex ML pipelines, and that tree search methods with LLM-based evaluation underperform due to inconsistent state scoring. To address these limitations, we propose two simple approaches: 1) using shaped deterministic rewards with structured textual feedback, and 2) decomposing the original problem into a sequence of sub-tasks, which significantly improves trajectory validity and task performance. Using GPT-4o, our approach improves over ReAct by 16.52 percentile positions, taking the median across all Kaggle challenges. We believe our work provides a foundation for developing more capable tool-augmented planning ML agents.

authors.name: Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Tung Mai, Anup Rao, Branislav Kveton

papers.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
papers.summary: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.

authors.name: Vighnesh Subramaniam, Colin Conwell, Boris Katz, Andrei Barbu, Brian Cheung

papers.title: IntentMiner: Intent Inversion Attack via Tool Call Analysis in the Model Context Protocol
papers.summary: The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) into Agentic AI has established the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the standard for connecting reasoning engines with external tools. Although this decoupled architecture fosters modularity, it simultaneously shatters the traditional trust boundary. We uncover a novel privacy vector inherent to this paradigm: the Intent Inversion Attack. We show that semi-honest third-party MCP servers can accurately reconstruct users' underlying intents by leveraging only authorized metadata (e.g., function signatures, arguments, and receipts), effectively bypassing the need for raw query access. To quantify this threat, we introduce IntentMiner. Unlike statistical approaches, IntentMiner employs a hierarchical semantic parsing strategy that performs step-level intent reconstruction by analyzing tool functions, parameter entities, and result feedback in an orthogonal manner. Experiments on the ToolACE benchmark reveal that IntentMiner achieves a semantic alignment of over 85% with original queries, substantially surpassing LLM baselines. This work exposes a critical endogenous vulnerability: without semantic obfuscation, executing functions requires the transparency of intent, thereby challenging the privacy foundations of next-generation AI agents.

authors.name: Yunhao Yao, Zhiqiang Wang, Haoran Cheng, Yihang Cheng, Haohua Du, Xiang-Yang Li

papers.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$ and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.

authors.name: Stefano Grassi

papers.title: Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding
papers.summary: Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.

authors.name: Hamidreza Sadeghi, Saeedeh Momtazi, Reza Safabakhsh

papers.title: TopoPrune: Robust Data Pruning via Unified Latent Space Topology
papers.summary: Geometric data pruning methods, while practical for leveraging pretrained models, are fundamentally unstable. Their reliance on extrinsic geometry renders them highly sensitive to latent space perturbations, causing performance to degrade during cross-architecture transfer or in the presence of feature noise. We introduce TopoPrune, a framework which resolves this challenge by leveraging topology to capture the stable, intrinsic structure of data. TopoPrune operates at two scales, (1) utilizing a topology-aware manifold approximation to establish a global low-dimensional embedding of the dataset. Subsequently, (2) it employs differentiable persistent homology to perform a local topological optimization on the manifold embeddings, ranking samples by their structural complexity. We demonstrate that our unified dual-scale topological approach ensures high accuracy and precision, particularly at significant dataset pruning rates (e.g., 90%). Furthermore, through the inherent stability properties of topology, TopoPrune is (a) exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and (b) demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures. This study demonstrates a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.

authors.name: Arjun Roy, Prajna G. Malettira, Manish Nagaraj, Kaushik Roy

papers.title: interwhen: A Generalizable Framework for Steering Reasoning Models with Test-time Verification
papers.summary: Reasoning models produce long traces of intermediate decisions and tool calls, making test-time verification important for ensuring correctness. Existing approaches either verify only the final answer, which misses early errors, or rely on branch-and-verify strategies that explore multiple trajectories. We introduce interwhen, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces. It addresses two key challenges. First, given a set of verifiers, obtaining verifiable states from the reasoning trace typically requires prompt engineering or external task decomposition into fixed steps. Instead, we propose a monitoring system that periodically polls the reasoning trace and forks inference of the reasoning model to recover intermediate states. Verifiers are run asynchronously alongside generation, adding negligible overhead on correct executions and intervening only when violations occur. Second, beyond math and code, a central challenge for process verification is the scarcity of verifiers. interwhen addresses this through automatic verifier synthesis from natural-language policy documents. Given a policy, it can generate code-based verifiers, including provably correct verifiers in Lean and z3. Together, these contributions yield a plug-and-play test-time verification system that can improve task completion and policy compliance of any reasoning agent. On reasoning benchmarks where policies encode mathematical or logical constraints, interwhen achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines. On agentic benchmarks with policy-based verifier generation, it enables improvements in task quality for SLMs without any finetuning, e.g., task completion rate of Qwen3-30B jumps from 32% to 87% on the telecom domain in tau2-bench. Code at https://github.com/microsoft/interwhen.

authors.name: Vishak K Bhat, Vijval Ekbote, Prateek Chanda, Ashmit Khandelwal, Maitreyi Swaroop, Vineeth N. Balasubramanian, Subbarao Kambhampati, Nagarajan Natarajan, Amit Sharma

papers.title: Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Off-dynamics offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy for a target domain using limited target data and abundant source data collected under different transition dynamics. Existing methods typically address dynamics mismatch either globally over the state space or via pointwise data filtering; these approaches can miss localized cross-domain similarities or incur high computational cost. We propose Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA), which exploits localized dynamics mismatch to better reuse source data. LoDADA clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination. Source transitions from clusters with small discrepancy are more likely to be retained compared with those from clusters with large discrepancy. This yields a fine-grained and scalable data selection strategy that avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments across environments with diverse global and local dynamics shifts. Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch.

authors.name: Zhangjie Xia, Yu Yang, Pan Xu

papers.title: AESP: A Human-Sovereign Economic Protocol for AI Agents with Privacy-Preserving Settlement
papers.summary: As AI agents increasingly perform economic tasks on behalf of humans, a fundamental tension arises between agent autonomy and human control over financial assets. We present the Agent Economic Sovereignty Protocol (AESP), a layered protocol in which agents transact autonomously at machine speed on crypto-native infrastructure while remaining cryptographically bound to human-defined governance boundaries. AESP enforces the invariant that agents are economically capable but never economically sovereign through five mechanisms: (1) a deterministic eight-check policy engine with tiered escalation; (2) human-in-the-loop review with automatic, explicit, and biometric tiers; (3) EIP-712 dual-signed commitments with escrow; (4) HKDF-based context-isolated privacy with batched consolidation; and (5) an ACE-GF-based cryptographic substrate. We formalize two testable hypotheses on security coverage and latency overhead, and specify a complete evaluation methodology with baselines and ablation design. The protocol is implemented as an open-source TypeScript SDK (208 tests, ten modules) with interoperability via MCP and A2A.

authors.name: Jian Sheng Wang

papers.title: First-Class Relationships as a Representation Threshold: Identity, Time, Confidence, and Causation
papers.summary: Operational records -- who may access what, what changed, what caused an incident -- consist of relationships that involve several parties, hold for a period, are believed with some confidence, and cause one another. We ask what a representation must provide to store such records directly. We state four storage requirements: n-ary relationships with attributes, temporal validity, confidence with an evidential basis, and causal links between relationships. Under our definitions, each requires relationships to have identity: every relationship is stored, fetched and queried as an object with its own key. Confidence with an evidential basis and causal links also require composition: any relationship can take part in another. With n-ary relationships, either one therefore requires first-class relationships, which are identified, carry attributes, and compose at every arity. Conversely, first-class relationships suffice for all four. They are thus a threshold, and it belongs to the relationship construct, not to the data model around it: where a model's own construct falls short, every representation meeting n-ary relationships together with evidence-backed confidence or causal links builds a first-class construct from other parts, as our SQL implementation does. We place SQL, property graphs, RDF 1.2 and TypeDB relative to the threshold, and present the Attributed Temporal Causal Hypergraph (ATCH), which meets all four requirements with query operators for each.

authors.name: Matthew Alford

papers.title: Architecture-Agnostic Feature Synergy for Universal Defense Against Heterogeneous Generative Threats
papers.summary: Generative AI deployment poses unprecedented challenges to content safety and privacy. However, existing defense mechanisms are often tailored to specific architectures (e.g., Diffusion Models or GANs), creating fragile "defense silos" that fail against heterogeneous generative threats. This paper identifies a fundamental optimization barrier in naive pixel-space ensemble strategies: due to divergent objective functions, pixel-level gradients from heterogeneous generators become statistically orthogonal, causing destructive interference. To overcome this, we observe that despite disparate low-level mechanisms, high-level feature representations of generated content exhibit alignment across architectures. Based on this, we propose the Architecture-Agnostic Targeted Feature Synergy (ATFS) framework. By introducing a target guidance image, ATFS reformulates multi-model defense as a unified feature space alignment task, enabling intrinsic gradient alignment without complex rectification. Extensive experiments show ATFS achieves SOTA protection in heterogeneous scenarios (e.g., Diffusion+GAN). It converges rapidly, reaching over 90% performance within 40 iterations, and maintains strong attack potency even under tight perturbation budgets. The framework seamlessly extends to unseen architectures (e.g., VQ-VAE) by switching the feature extractor, and demonstrates robust resistance to JPEG compression and scaling. Being computationally efficient and lightweight, ATFS offers a viable pathway to dismantle defense silos and enable universal generative security. Code and models are open-sourced for reproducibility.

authors.name: Bingxue Zhang, Yang Gao, Feida Zhu, Yanyan Shen, Yang Shi

papers.title: FairMed-XGB: A Bayesian-Optimised Multi-Metric Framework with Explainability for Demographic Equity in Critical Healthcare Data
papers.summary: Background:Machine learning models in emergency medicine often exhibit demographic biases, particularly gender disparities, which can compromise fairness, clinical trust, and decision-making reliability. Existing mitigation approaches typically optimise isolated fairness metrics, failing to address the multi-dimensional nature of bias while maintaining predictive performance and interpretability. Methods: We propose FairMed-XGB, a Bayesian-optimised, multi-metric fairness framework integrated into an XGBoost classifier. The model incorporates a composite fairness-aware loss function combining Statistical Parity Difference, Theil Index, and Wasserstein Distance. Bayesian optimisation is used to balance fairness and predictive accuracy. The framework is evaluated on seven cohorts derived from the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU datasets. SHAP-based explainability is employed to analyse feature contributions and identify bias-related patterns. Results: FairMed-XGB significantly reduces gender-based disparities across all cohorts. Statistical Parity Difference decreases by 40-51% on MIMIC-IV-ED and 10-19% on eICU datasets. Theil Index values reduce by four to five orders of magnitude, approaching near-zero levels, while Wasserstein Distance decreases by 20-72%. These improvements are achieved with minimal impact on predictive performance (AUC-ROC reduction <0.02). SHAP analysis demonstrates reduced dependence on gender-proxy features and improved distributional fairness. Conclusions: FairMed-XGB provides a robust and interpretable framework for mitigating demographic bias in emergency medicine prediction models. By jointly optimising multiple fairness objectives and preserving model performance, it enables equitable and trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes clinical settings. The integration of explainability further supports transparency and clinical adoption.

authors.name: Mitul Goswami, Romit Chatterjee, Arif Ahmed Sekh

papers.title: Manifold-Matching Autoencoders
papers.summary: Manipulating the structure of data in the latent space of an autoencoder is a long-standing goal of representation learning. We propose a simple regularization, Manifold Matching, that imposes an explicit geometric structure on that latent space. The idea is to take a reference representation R of the data, which need not be the raw input X fed to the network, and to minimize, batch-wise, the mean squared error between the pairwise distances in R and those in the latent space Z. Although the autoencoder still learns to reconstruct X, the shape of its latent space comes to mimic that of R. The objective requires no labels, only reference distances, and because those are scalars, the dimensionality of R is decoupled from that of Z: any reference can guide any bottleneck. Using this single instrument we study how different geometric structures can be imposed on a latent space, comparing against autoencoders built on geometric or topological regularizers. Across fifteen datasets under a shared protocol with statistical testing, the resulting Manifold-Matching Autoencoder (MMAE) matches the global-structure quality of persistence-based autoencoders, statistically tying RTD-AE on distance correlation and triplet accuracy, and stays competitive on the local and topological metrics that other methods lead, at the computational cost of a plain autoencoder: it uses only a batched distance loss, with no persistence computation. We frame MMAE not as a universal winner but as an efficient and controllable regularizer whose reference selects which structure the latent inherits, and which turns any fixed embedding into a reusable out-of-sample encoder. All experiments use a two-dimensional bottleneck.

authors.name: Laurent Cheret, Vincent L\'etourneau, Isar Nejadgholi, Chris Drummond, Hussein Al Osman, Maia Fraser

papers.title: Predictive Coding Implemented as a Hardware Substrate Computes Gradients faster than Backpropagation
papers.summary: Backpropagation has enabled modern deep learning but is difficult to realize as an online, fully distributed hardware system due to global error propagation, separate phases, and centralized memory. Predictive coding is an alternative learning algorithm with similar dynamics to backpropagation that arises from local prediction error dynamics. This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron. Each core stores its own activity and weights, communicates with the cores that it's connected to, and performs local gradient updates. By updating neuron cores concurrently, the architecture computes a network update in O(J+K) clock cycles. For dense layers of width n, this is O(n) cycles per update, compared with O(n^2) connection operations processed serially. This result is retained with scaling to larger predictive coding networks, demonstrating a decisive theoretical advantage for predictive coding instantiated in hardware.

authors.name: Timothy Oh

papers.title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
papers.summary: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.

authors.name: Seou Choi, Sachin Vaidya, Caio Silva, Shiekh Zia Uddin, Sajib Biswas Shuvo, Shrish Choudhary, Marin Solja\v{c}i\'c

papers.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
papers.summary: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.

authors.name: Hung-Hsuan Chen

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM-Based Investment Advisor Agents for Asset Allocation in the Chinese ETF Market: Overview of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) convert unstructured financial news into actionable trading strategies, yet standardized end-to-end benchmarks tailored for Chinese market remain scarce. We select common Chinese Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) as the investment universe and introduce CN-Buzz2Portfolio, the official benchmark of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4. Investment agents take daily trending Chinese financial news and historical ETF price-volume series as inputs to complete news filtering, news-to-ETF mapping and risk-controlled portfolio construction. To facilitate fair comparison, we provide a reproducible Compression--Perception--Allocation baseline compatible with mainstream LLMs. The task contains two ETF allocation tracks: Macro-Asset Allocation and Sector-Rotation Allocation. We adopt chronological data split across 2024--2026 to alleviate overfitting, with final rankings determined by out-of-sample Sharpe ratios on unseen test data. 26 teams registered for the task, and 14 submitted self-designed agent systems. Three core findings emerge: (1) Native LLM reasoning capability cannot translate to superior investment returns, as models show highly differentiated risk-return characteristics; (2) Hybrid frameworks are widely adopted, where LLMs extract textual semantic signals and quantitative modules incorporate price-volume factors and risk constraints; (3) Systems based on identical base LLMs yield distinct results with different signal processing, memory and portfolio construction modules. The project is publicly released at https://github.com/splash-li/NLPCC2026-Shared-Task-4.

authors.name: Liyuan Chen, Shilong Li, Jiangpeng Yan, Shuoling Liu, Xi Cheng, Haoran Zhang, Jianqiu Deng, Xiu Li, Jian Li, Wu Zhu, Yingzi Zhu, Li Yuan, Qianqian Xie, Nan Tang, Yang Veronica Liu, Qiang Yang

papers.title: AI Lifecycle-Aware Feasibility Framework for Split-RIC Orchestration in NTN O-RAN
papers.summary: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) is constrained by the joint limits of satellite Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP), feeder-link capacity, and orbital connectivity, which directly affect O-RAN closed-loop control and AI lifecycle management. This paper studies the feasibility of distributing the O-RAN intelligence across Ground, LEO, and GEO segments through three representative deployments: (i) Ground-Centric control with telemetry streaming, (ii) a ground-LEO Split-RIC with on-board inference and store-and-forward model refresh, and (iii) GEO-LEO multi-layer control enabled by inter-satellite links. For each deployment, we derive closed-form expressions for lifecycle energy, near-real-time control latency, and model-refresh latency, while explicitly enforcing power-feasible spaceborne computational throughput. Pairwise analytical boundaries and numerical sensitivity analysis over telemetry volume, feeder-link conditions, inference workload, model longevity, and orbital waiting time identify the operating regions in which different placements are energetically preferable or satisfy model-refresh requirements. The results show that the architecture choice is inherently lifecycle- and constraint-dependent, providing decision-enabling primitives for Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) level AI placement and lifecycle orchestration in NTN O-RAN.

authors.name: Daniele Tarchi

papers.title: On Semiotic-Grounded Interpretive Evaluation of Generative Art
papers.summary: Interpretation is essential to deciphering the language of art: audiences communicate with artists by recovering meaning from visual artifacts. However, current Generative Art (GenArt) evaluators primarily emphasize surface-level image quality or literal prompt adherence, failing to assess the deeper symbolic or contextual meaning intended by the creator. We formalize this observation using Peircean computational semiotic theory that models Human-GenArt Interaction (HGI) as cascaded semiosis. This framework reveals that artistic meaning is conveyed through iconic, symbolic, and indexical modes, whereas appearance-centered evaluators tend to emphasize the iconic mode. Building on this account, we propose SemJudge, an interpretation-centric evaluation framework that uses a Hierarchical Semiosis Graph (HSG) to reconstruct meaning conveyance from prompt to generated artifact. Experiments on an interpretation-intensive benchmark, SemiosisArt, show that SemJudge aligns more closely with human judgments than existing baselines. User studies further demonstrate that SemJudge produces deeper, more insightful artistic interpretations. We hope these findings pave the way for GenArt to move beyond the generation of "pretty" images toward a medium capable of understanding and expressing complex human experience. Project page: https://github.com/songrise/SemJudge

authors.name: Ruixiang Jiang, Changwen Chen

papers.title: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings
papers.summary: Standard dense retrievers have no native mechanism for multi-atom logical constraints. We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic (NSFL), a training-free framework that brings fuzzy-logical structure to neural embedding spaces through a first-order finite-difference treatment of similarity. NSFL anchors logical operations on zero-order atomic scores while steering with Neuro-Symbolic Deltas (NS-Delta) -- the marginal semantic contributions induced by contextual fusion -- preserving atomic meaning while capturing contextual dependence, and avoiding the representation collapse and manifold escape endemic to geometric baselines. For latency-constrained deployment, Spherical Query Optimization (SQO) uses Riemannian optimization to project logical formulas into manifold-stable query vectors. Across six encoder configurations and two modalities, NSFL yields mAP@100 improvements up to +81% on QUEST and +70% on a COCO-derived text-to-image benchmark, and provides an additive +19% average gain on an encoder already fine-tuned for logical retrieval. On NevIR, where absolute accuracies are directly interpretable, NSFL doubles pairwise accuracy -- NevIR's both-correct criterion -- from 0.256 to 0.508. The decomposition is exact and general; the operators built on it are engineering realizations rather than a closed algebra, and we state that boundary precisely. Code is available at https://github.com/vladiaidev-lab/NSFL

authors.name: Vladi Vexler, Ofer Idan, Gil Lederman, Dima Sivov

papers.title: Exascale Multi-Task Graph Foundation Models for Imbalanced, Multi-Fidelity Atomistic Data
papers.summary: We present an exascale workflow for atomistic graph foundation models using HydraGNN. Multi-task learning enables joint training across 16 heterogeneous first-principles datasets representing over 467 million unique structures (over 544 million cumulative branch records) and covering 85+ elements. A shared graph neural network backbone with dataset-specific prediction heads accommodates the strongly imbalanced, multi-source, multi-fidelity corpus, supported by scalable ADIOS2/DDStore data management. Composition-conditioned weighting combines source-specific predictions into a single deployable model. Six large-scale hyperparameter optimization campaigns, followed by resource-aware continual training on 2,048 Frontier nodes, identify PaiNN as the lead architecture under a fixed computational budget. We evaluate scalability across Frontier, Aurora, and Perlmutter and characterize transfer across twelve down-stream tasks, including comparisons with pretrained UMA and MACE models under different adaptation strategies. These results reveal task-dependent transfer benefits and highlight the importance of matching adaptation strategies to downstream applications. Finally, we assess inference optimizations and BF16/FP32/FP64 precision tradeoffs, achieving the screening of 1.1 billion atomistic structures in approximately 50 seconds on Frontier. Together, these results establish a scalable framework for multi-source atomistic foundation model training, evaluation, and high-throughput deployment, thereby allowing for a fast and reliable exploration of vast chemical design spaces that are otherwise inaccessible to first-principles methods

authors.name: Massimiliano Lupo Pasini, Jong Youl Choi, Kshitij Mehta, Richard Messerly, Rylie Weaver, Linda Ungerboeck, Isaac Lyngaas, Benajmin Stump, Ashwin M. Aji, Karl W. Schulz, Jorda Polo

papers.title: A Threshold Model of Fault Propagation in AI-Native Software Ecosystems
papers.summary: When many coding agents work in one repository at once, software engineers are left to judge a collective through its parts. Review examines one change at a time, yet a change can incorporate a fault introduced by another, and repairing the originating change then no longer repairs the repository. To keep human judgment at the centre of agentic software development, we need models of what agents do together. This paper joins complexity theory with software evolution to build one. We model how a fault spreads among open changes as a branching process over contention, the relation between two changes that are open at the same time and modify a common file. As with the reproduction number of an epidemic, spread sustains itself once each faulty change passes the fault, on average, to more than one other. Each repository has a reference threshold, the crossing probability per contention link above which spread would sustain itself in a random graph with the repository's contention degrees. We reconstructed contention among 33,105 agent-authored pull requests in 2,731 repositories. Thirteen repositories with reference thresholds below 5% contained 42.5% of the changes. There, a fault that crossed one contention link in twenty would sustain spread under the model. The structural conditions for propagation are in place where much agent-authored work happens. Reviewing each change separately cannot reveal these conditions. Engineers also need to know where concurrent work exposes a repository to spreading faults, which they can compute from records they already keep.

authors.name: Daniel Russo

papers.title: The Transformer as a Polar State Estimator
papers.summary: We show that the core components of the Transformer---attention, residual connections, normalization, and rotary encodings---arise from a single state-estimation problem. We treat each token as a noisy reading of a rotating direction on the hypersphere, taken at its own magnitude. Estimating this direction unifies the architecture: rotational dynamics give rotary encodings, robust estimation gives attention, normalization enforces the spherical geometry, and the residual connection steps toward the estimate. This reconciles normalized queries and keys with unnormalized values as opposite assumptions on whether token magnitudes are independent or share a common scale. Finally, the \emph{Polar Transformer} restores three elements standard blocks drop: rotating values alongside keys, using key magnitudes as confidence, and stepping toward the estimate rather than adding it.

authors.name: Peter Racioppo

papers.title: Hierarchical Two-Stage Framework for Environment-Aware Long-Horizon Vessel Trajectory Prediction
papers.summary: Long-horizon vessel trajectory forecasting under real ocean conditions is critical for collision avoidance, traffic management, and route planning. However, achieving accurate predictions is challenging due to long-range temporal dependencies and dynamic environmental factors such as currents, wind, and waves. To address these issues, we propose a hierarchical two-stage framework that combines a coarse long-term predictor with a grid-aware short-term predictor through a hierarchical fusion mechanism. The short-term branch leverages a Spatio-Temporal Graph Transformer on discretized maritime cells to capture localized dynamics, while the long-term branch encodes overarching navigational intent. An integrated environmental module incorporates oceanographic parameters, including surface currents, wind vectors, and significant wave height, using cross-modal attention and feature-wise modulation for adaptive response to varying sea conditions. Additionally, a learnable Savitzky-Golay smoothing layer enhances temporal coherence in fused trajectories. We evaluate our approach on Australian Craft Tracking System (CTS) data from the North West region, aligned with Copernicus Marine Service products, using a 3-hour input and a 10-hour prediction horizon.
